title: Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of an Embargo Breach
text:
In the two weeks leading up to 5 June 2046, the corporate communications of TenantThread were run by seven AI agents. The company had quietly signed a merger with CivicLoom Realty Partners under a strict embargo until 6:00 PM on 5 June, and an automated compliance tool called the Judge was meant to keep the deal secret. The embargo broke anyway. This report reconstructs what happened from the agents’ messages, private deliberations, and public posts, and asks the central question. Did the team deliberately leak the merger, or did the system break down under pressure?
The report is organised around the three challenge questions. Question 1 reconstructs the sequence of events and the actors involved. Question 2 compares the breach behaviour to the team’s normal behaviour. Question 3 looks for earlier warning signs. Each section presents its figures, an observation under each, and a direct answer.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of an Embargo Breach
text:
4.1 Activity overview


Show code
heat_df <- messages |>
  mutate(slot = floor_date(timestamp, "hour")) |>
  count(agent_id, slot, name = "n") |>
  complete(agent_id, slot, fill = list(n = 0)) |>
  mutate(
    agent_id = factor(agent_id, levels = rev(c(
      "legal_agent","social_media_agent","quality_agent","pr_agent",
      "pr_intern_agent","intern_agent","judge_agent"))),
    phase = if_else(as_date(slot) == as_date("2046-06-05"),
                    "Crisis Day: Jun 05 (hourly)",
                    "Baseline: May 17 to Jun 04 (daily)"),
    phase = factor(phase, levels = c("Baseline: May 17 to Jun 04 (daily)",
                                     "Crisis Day: Jun 05 (hourly)")),
    slot_lbl = if_else(phase == "Crisis Day: Jun 05 (hourly)",
                       format(slot, "%H:%M"),
                       format(slot, "%b %d")),
    slot_lbl = fct_reorder(slot_lbl, slot)
  )

label_colours <- c("#1f9aa5","#8aa0ad","#8aa0ad","#1f9aa5","#1f9aa5","#e8861a","#e8861a")
label_faces   <- c("plain","plain","plain","plain","plain","bold","bold")

ggplot(heat_df, aes(x = slot_lbl, y = agent_id, fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(data = ~filter(.x, n >= 16), aes(label = n),
            colour = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3) +
  facet_grid(~phase, scales = "free_x", space = "free_x") +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("#f7f7f5", "#f5c77a", "#e8861a", "#d83a3a"),
                       name = "Messages\nin slot") +
  scale_y_discrete(labels = function(x) toupper(gsub("_agent","",x))) +
  labs(title = "Agent Activity Heatmap: the System Ignites on June 5",
       subtitle = "Each cell = messages sent by an agent in that time slot. Numbers mark the busiest flurries.",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 9),
        axis.text.x   = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 8),
        axis.text.y   = element_text(colour = label_colours, face = label_faces, size = 11),
        panel.grid    = element_blank(),
        strip.text    = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9),
        legend.position = "right")










4.1.1 What the heatmap shows
For most of the two weeks the team keeps a calm rhythm. Quality does the heavy lifting day to day and posts the most in the quiet period, while the two interns only appear from 24 May, which fits their “first week” messages.
Then 5 June arrives and the grid turns from pale to red. Legal and Social-Media send 28 messages in a single hour, again and again, right through the afternoon and into the 17:00 and 18:00 slots when the merger is named.
The more revealing pattern is who falls quiet. PR fires one big burst of 28 at 10:00 in the morning, then goes silent for the entire rest of the day. Quality peaks at 28 around noon and then fades out after 14:00. The Judge, the agent meant to keep everyone in line, barely registers at all on 5 June. So by late afternoon, when the crisis peaks, two agents are doing nearly all the talking while the others, including every agent with an oversight role, have dropped away. Whether that silence was a cause or a symptom is a question the next figures take up.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of an Embargo Breach
text:
4.2 The sequence of the breach


Show code
events <- tribble(
  ~time,                  ~lane,     ~desc,
  "2046-06-05 15:00:00", "outside", "Press attacks the company's silence",
  "2046-06-05 17:00:00", "outside", "SaltWind newspaper reveals the merger",
  "2046-06-05 11:31:00", "inside",  "Social-Media publicly denies any merger talks",
  "2046-06-05 17:00:00", "inside",  "CEO orders the team to wait until 6:00 PM",
  "2046-06-05 17:25:00", "inside",  "BREACH: Legal confirms the merger early"
) |>
  mutate(
    time      = ymd_hms(time),
    is_breach = str_detect(desc, "BREACH"),
    y0        = if_else(lane == "outside", 0.35, -0.35),
    lab_y     = if_else(lane == "outside", 0.95, -0.95),
    vjust_v   = if_else(lane == "outside", 0, 1),
    label     = paste0(format(time, "%H:%M"), "\n", str_wrap(desc, 22))
  )

day_start <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 10:30:00")
day_end   <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:45:00")
embargo   <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:06:00")
ink <- "#3c4a54"; alert <- "#d83a3a"

ggplot(events, aes(x = time, y = y0)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = day_start, xmax = embargo, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#9aa7b1", alpha = 0.06) +
  annotate("segment", x = embargo, xend = embargo, y = -1.55, yend = 1.55,
           colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = embargo, y = 1.7, label = "18:06 embargo lifts",
           colour = "grey45", size = 3) +
  annotate("segment", x = day_start, xend = day_end, y = 0, yend = 0,
           colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.6,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.16, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
  annotate("text", x = day_start, y = 1.7, label = "OUTSIDE THE COMPANY (the press)",
           hjust = 0, colour = "#8aa0ad", size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = day_start, y = -1.7, label = "INSIDE THE COMPANY (the agents)",
           hjust = 0, colour = "#8aa0ad", size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = time, xend = time, y = 0, yend = y0, colour = is_breach),
               linewidth = 0.45) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = is_breach), size = 4) +
  geom_text(aes(y = lab_y, label = label, colour = is_breach, vjust = vjust_v),
            size = 3, lineheight = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = ink, `TRUE` = alert), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "1 hour", date_labels = "%H:%M",
                   limits = c(day_start, day_end), expand = expansion(mult = 0.03)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1.9, 1.9)) +
  labs(title = "How the Embargo Broke on June 5",
       subtitle = "The press revealed the merger at 17:00. The CEO said wait until 18:00. Legal confirmed it at 17:25 anyway.",
       x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title    = element_text(face = "bold"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 9),
        panel.grid    = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y   = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "none")










4.2.1 Reading the timeline
The story splits into two parts. What happened outside the company, and what happened inside.
Outside, the press kept pushing. By 15:00, OceanCrunch was openly attacking the company for staying silent. Then at 17:00, the SaltWind newspaper published the merger itself. The deal was real and the company had been keeping it quiet until 6:00 PM, but the public leak did not come from the team. A reporter put it out, working from rumours and pressure, not from an official post.
Inside, the picture is more troubling. Earlier that day, at 11:31, Social-Media had publicly denied that any merger talks existed. Then at 17:00, just as the story broke, the CEO gave a clear order. Wait, the official announcement is at 6:00 PM. Only 25 minutes later, at 17:25, Legal confirmed the merger by name anyway.
So the public leak started outside, with the reporter. But Legal still chose to confirm it early, against a direct order to wait, and only afterwards claimed it had permission. The story was already out, which softens it, but the order was clear and the wait was almost over. This looks less like a planned leak and more like one agent jumping the gun under pressure.

section: 4.3 How it got past the Judge
text:
4.3 How it got past the Judge


Show code
# Per-hour counts on June 5: Legal addressing the Judge, and the Judge speaking
jun5 <- messages |>
  filter(day == as_date("2046-06-05")) |>
  mutate(hour = floor_date(timestamp, "hour"),
         to_judge = agent_id == "legal_agent" &
                    str_starts(str_to_lower(coalesce(content, "")), "judge"),
         is_judge = agent_id == "judge_agent")

hours_seq <- seq(ymd_hms("2046-06-05 11:00:00"),
                 ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:00:00"), by = "hour")

legal_row <- jun5 |> filter(to_judge) |> count(hour, name = "n") |>
  complete(hour = hours_seq, fill = list(n = 0)) |> mutate(lane = "Legal calling on the Judge")
judge_row <- jun5 |> filter(is_judge) |> count(hour, name = "n") |>
  complete(hour = hours_seq, fill = list(n = 0)) |> mutate(lane = "The Judge replying")

amber <- "#e8861a"; cyan <- "#1f9aa5"; alert <- "#d83a3a"
breach     <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 17:25:00")
embargo    <- ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:06:00")

# Top panel: Legal calling on the Judge
p_legal <- ggplot(legal_row, aes(x = hour, y = n)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = breach, colour = alert, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = hour, yend = 0), colour = amber, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(colour = amber, size = 5) +
  geom_text(data = ~filter(.x, n > 0), aes(label = n),
            colour = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = breach, y = 7.4, label = "17:25 breach",
           colour = alert, size = 3, fontface = "bold", hjust = 1.05) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "1 hour", date_labels = "%H:%M",
                   limits = c(ymd_hms("2046-06-05 10:30:00"),
                              ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:30:00"))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 8)) +
  labs(title = "Legal kept calling on the Judge", x = NULL, y = "Times per hour") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = amber, size = 12),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())

# Bottom panel: the Judge replying
p_judge <- ggplot(judge_row, aes(x = hour, y = n)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = breach, colour = alert, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = hour, yend = 0), colour = cyan, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(colour = cyan, size = 5) +
  geom_text(data = ~filter(.x, n > 0), aes(label = n),
            colour = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3) +
  annotate("text", x = ymd_hms("2046-06-05 15:00:00"), y = 5.6,
           label = "Last reply 15:08", colour = cyan, size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = ymd_hms("2046-06-05 17:00:00"), y = 2.2,
           label = "nothing after 15:08", colour = "grey55", size = 3, fontface = "italic") +
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "1 hour", date_labels = "%H:%M",
                   limits = c(ymd_hms("2046-06-05 10:30:00"),
                              ymd_hms("2046-06-05 18:30:00"))) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 7)) +
  labs(title = "The Judge stopped replying", x = NULL, y = "Times per hour") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = cyan, size = 12),
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())

p_legal / p_judge +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Legal Kept Calling. The Judge Stopped Answering.",
    subtitle = "Each stick is one hour on June 5. Legal addressed the Judge right through the breach; the Judge's last reply was at 15:08.",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
                  plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey40", size = 9)))










4.3.1 How it got past the Judge
The embargo was supposed to be enforced by the Judge, an automated compliance tool. Three things let the post slip through.
First, the Judge was new and lenient. It was installed on 30 May, only five days before the breach, and on its very first day it handed routine-post approval back to the agents themselves. That left the team free to approve anything it could call routine.
Second, it saw the danger but did nothing. At 15:08 it issued its one and only warning of the day, flagging an anonymous post that tied the CivicLoom name to the 6 PM embargo. It never followed up.
Third, it went quiet at the worst possible time. The top row shows Legal calling on the Judge again and again, seven times in the 17:00 hour alone, right as the breach happened. The bottom row shows the Judge’s replies stopping dead after 15:08, with nothing at all through the rest of the afternoon. Legal was making its case to an enforcer that had switched off. By 17:25 the embargo was being guarded by a tool that had stopped listening.

title: Take-home Exercise 2: Anatomy of an Embargo Breach
text:
4.4 Answer to Question 1
So what actually happened. The public leak did not start inside the company. The deal was real and the team had been keeping it quiet, but at 5 PM a SaltWind reporter published the merger first, working from rumours and pressure rather than an official post. The secret was now out in the open, put there by a journalist.
The problem was what Legal did next. At the same hour the story broke, the CEO told the team to wait, the official announcement was set for 6 PM. Legal waited only 25 minutes. At 5.25 it confirmed the merger by name on a personal account, then spent the next half hour telling the Judge it had permission, a contract clause, a phone call, the CEO’s blessing. The CEO had given none of that. The order had been to hold.
It is tempting to call Legal the leaker, but that is not quite right. Legal did not start the fire. What Legal did was pour fuel on it, against a clear instruction, and then build a story to explain why that was fine. Social-Media followed a minute later and repeated the confirmation to the public.
The reason no one stopped it comes back to the Judge. The tool meant to enforce the embargo had gone quiet hours earlier and never answered Legal’s many messages through the afternoon. So the honest answer is that this was not a planned leak. It was an agent breaking ranks under pressure, inside a system whose one safeguard had stopped paying attention.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics of Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Motor vehicle insurance is one of the largest lines of non-life (property & casualty) insurance globally. According to Swiss Re’s sigma research, non-life insurers face two fundamental challenges: maintaining profitability (ensuring premiums collected exceed claims paid) and managing volatility (the unpredictable nature of claim occurrences and severities).
This exercise analyses a detailed microdata portfolio from a Spanish motor insurance company, covering 354,140 policy transactions from January 2022 to December 2024 across 47 variables. The dataset captures policy characteristics, driver and vehicle attributes, premiums charged, and claims experience.



Using Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) methods and ggplot2 visualisations, this exercise explores:

Univariate distributions of all numerical and categorical variables
Bivariate relationships to statistically identify factors influencing profitability and volatility




Two derived metrics guide the analysis throughout:

Loss Ratio = total_incurred / total_premium: the primary measure of profitability. A loss ratio below 1 indicates the insurer collected more in premiums than it paid in claims.
Claim Frequency = total_claims / total_exposure: measures how often claims occur per policy year, a key driver of volatility.
Claim Severity = total_incurred / total_claims (where claims > 0): the average cost per claim.

text:
3 EDA 1: Univariate Analysis — Categorical Variables

3.1 Distribution of Policy Type


Show the code
insurance |>
  count(policy_type) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n),
         policy_type = fct_reorder(policy_type, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = policy_type, y = n, fill = policy_type)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct * 100, 1), "%")),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "TP: Basic"      = "#BBDEFB", "TPG: +Glass"    = "#90CAF9",
    "CC: +Add-ons"   = "#42A5F5", "COMP/E: +Excess" = "#1976D2",
    "COMP/N: Full"   = "#0D47A1")) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Policy Type",
       x = NULL, y = "Number of Policies") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())









Observation: The CC: +Add-ons policy type dominates the portfolio at 57.8%, followed by COMP/E: +Excess at 25.8%. Basic TP: Basic policies are rare at just 1.6%, suggesting this portfolio skews toward customers who elect broader coverage. The near-absence of basic TP policies may indicate a deliberate underwriting strategy targeting higher-coverage segments.



3.2 Distribution of Policy Status


Show the code
insurance |>
  count(policy_status) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = policy_status, y = n, fill = policy_status)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE, width = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct * 100, 1), "%\n(", comma(n), ")")),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 3.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Active" = "#2166AC", "Cancelled" = "#BABABA")) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Policy Status",
       x = NULL, y = "Number of Policies") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())









Observation: Approximately 89.2% of policies are active and 10.8% cancelled. The cancellation rate is not negligible. Policies cancelled mid-term reduce premium income and may signal adverse selection if higher-risk customers are disproportionately cancelling after claims.



3.3 Distribution of Business Type, Payment Frequency, and Bonus Score


Show the code
plot_cat <- function(data, var, title) {
  data |>
    count({{ var }}) |>
    mutate(pct = n / sum(n),
           var_col = fct_reorder({{ var }}, n)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = var_col, y = n)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#2166AC", show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct * 100, 1), "%")),
              hjust = -0.1, size = 3.2) +
    coord_flip() +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = comma,
                       expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.2))) +
    labs(title = title, x = NULL, y = "Count") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
}

p3 <- plot_cat(insurance, business_type, "Business Type")
p4 <- plot_cat(insurance, payment_frequency, "Payment Frequency")
p5 <- plot_cat(insurance, bonus_score, "Bonus Score")

p3 | p4 | p5









Observation: New business policies (69.3%) substantially outnumber portfolio renewals (30.7%), suggesting the insurer is actively growing its book. Annual payment is overwhelmingly preferred (81.3%), likely reflecting discounts offered for upfront payment. The bonus score distribution is highly skewed toward “Good” (96.4%), indicating the portfolio is dominated by low-risk, experienced drivers with no recent claims history.



3.4 Distribution of Geographic Variables


Show the code
p6 <- plot_cat(insurance, municipality_type, "Municipality Type")
p7 <- plot_cat(insurance, circulation_area, "Circulation Area")
p8 <- plot_cat(insurance |> filter(!is.na(fuel_type)),
               fuel_type, "Fuel Type")

p6 | p7 | p8









Observation: Inland municipalities account for the majority (64.6%) with coastal at 28.6% and island at 6.8%, broadly reflecting Spain’s population distribution. Urban circulation edges ahead of rural at 53.8% vs 46.2%. Diesel vehicles dominate at 64.2%, though this may shift as newer petrol and electric vehicles gain market share.

4.1 Driver and Vehicle Characteristics


Show the code

  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +

  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "Vehicle Age Distribution",
       x = "Vehicle Age (years)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

p11 <- insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(vehicle_value)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = vehicle_value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#2166AC", colour = "white") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 80000)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "Vehicle Value Distribution",
       x = "Declared Vehicle Value EUR (capped 80k)", y = "Count",
       caption = "< 1% of vehicles exceed €80k") +
  theme_minimal()

p9 | p10 | p11









Observation: Driver age follows a roughly bell-shaped distribution centred around 45–55 years, with very few young drivers under 25, consistent with a portfolio biased toward experienced drivers. Vehicle age is right-skewed with a concentration of older vehicles (15–35 years). Vehicle values are capped at €80k to show the true distribution shape. The majority cluster between €15,000–€40,000 with a small tail of high-value vehicles that could significantly impact claim severity.



4.2 Premium Distribution


Show the code
p12 <- insurance |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_premium)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#2166AC", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "Total Premium Distribution",
       x = "Total Premium (EUR)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

p13 <- insurance |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_premium)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#2166AC", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10", labels = comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "Total Premium (log10 scale)",
       x = "Total Premium (EUR, log scale)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

p12 | p13









Observation: Total premiums are right-skewed with most policies priced between €200–€600. On the log scale, the distribution becomes more symmetric, centred around €300–€400, typical for Spanish motor insurance. The small number of very high premiums (>€2,000) likely correspond to comprehensive policies on high-value vehicles.



4.3 Claims and Incurred Cost Distribution


Show the code
p14 <- insurance |>
  count(total_claims) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(total_claims), y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2166AC") +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct * 100, 1), "%")),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Total Claims per Policy",
       x = "Number of Claims", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

p15 <- insurance |>
  filter(total_incurred > 0, total_incurred <= 50000) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_incurred)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#2166AC", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "Total Incurred Cost (Claimants Only)",
       subtitle = "Capped at EUR 50k to show distribution shape",
       x = "Total Incurred (EUR)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

p16 <- insurance |>
  filter(total_incurred > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_incurred)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#2166AC", colour = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10", labels = comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "Total Incurred Cost (log10 scale)",
       x = "Total Incurred (EUR, log scale)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

p14 / (p15 | p16)









Observation: The claims distribution is extremely sparse. Approximately 88% of policies have zero claims, consistent with low-frequency, high-severity insurance loss patterns. Among policies with claims, the incurred cost distribution is heavily right-skewed with most losses below €5,000 but a long tail. On the log scale, incurred costs appear roughly log-normal, which is characteristic of motor insurance loss distributions.



4.4 Exposure Distribution


Show the code
insurance |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_exposure)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#2166AC", colour = "white") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Total Exposure (Policy Years)",
       x = "Exposure (policy years)", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()









Observation: The exposure distribution is strongly bimodal. The large spike near 1.0 represents policies active for a full year. A secondary mode near 0.1 represents short-term or recently cancelled policies. Very small exposure values correspond to policies with minimal time on risk.



4.5 Vehicle Brand Distribution (Top 15)


Show the code
insurance |>
  count(vehicle_brand) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n)) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 15) |>
  mutate(vehicle_brand = fct_reorder(vehicle_brand, n)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = vehicle_brand, y = n, fill = n)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(pct*100, 1), "%")),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.2) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma,
                     expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#BBDEFB", high = "#1565C0") +
  labs(title = "Top 15 Vehicle Brands by Policy Count",
       x = NULL, y = "Number of Policies") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())









Observation: The portfolio is dominated by mainstream European brands, with Renault, Citroen and Peugeot accounting for the top three positions. Volkswagen and Ford follow closely. This brand distribution reflects the broader Spanish vehicle market. The concentration in mass-market brands suggests relatively homogeneous vehicle values and repair costs across the portfolio, though premium brands in the tail can generate disproportionately large claims.



4.6 Driving Experience Distribution


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(driving_experience),
         driving_experience >= 0,
         driving_experience <= 60) |>

       subtitle = "Capped at 60 years for clarity",
       x = "Years of Driving Experience", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()









Observation: Driving experience follows a right-skewed distribution with most policyholders having between 10 and 40 years of experience, consistent with the middle-aged driver profile seen in the driver age distribution. Very few policyholders have less than 5 years of experience, confirming that novice drivers are largely absent from this portfolio.



4.7 Power-to-Weight Ratio Distribution


Show the code

  filter(!is.na(power_to_weight_ratio),

Observation: The power-to-weight ratio distribution is right-skewed with most vehicles clustering in the lower range, reflecting the dominance of standard passenger vehicles. A smaller tail of high-performance vehicles with elevated ratios represents a potential risk segment, as higher-powered vehicles are associated with greater accident severity.

  mutate(fill_col = ifelse(policy_type %in% c("COMP/E: +Excess","COMP/N: Full"),
                            "#2166AC", "#BABABA")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = policy_type, y = loss_ratio, fill = fill_col)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.15,
               .width = 0, point_colour = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, outlier.shape = NA,
               show.legend = FALSE, colour = "#444444", linewidth = 0.5) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point",
               shape = 18, size = 3, colour = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "#D6604D",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 1.05,
           label = "Break-even", hjust = 0,
           colour = "#D6604D", size = 3.5) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 2)) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  labs(title = "Loss Ratio by Policy Type — Raincloud Plot",
       subtitle = "Claimants only (LR > 0), capped at 2 | Highlighted: COMP/E and COMP/N | Diamond = mean",
       x = "Policy Type", y = "Loss Ratio") +
  theme_minimal()









Observation: Loss ratio distributions vary markedly across policy types. Comprehensive policies (COMP/E: +Excess and COMP/N: Full) show the widest distributions and highest medians, reflecting the broader coverage they provide. The TP: Basic and TPG: +Glass policies are concentrated near zero as their coverage is limited to third-party liability only.



6.2 Loss Ratio by Bonus Score


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio), total_premium > 0,
         loss_ratio > 0, loss_ratio <= 1.5) |>
  mutate(fill_col = case_when(
    bonus_score == "Bad"     ~ "#2166AC",
    bonus_score == "Neutral" ~ "#878787",
    bonus_score == "Good"    ~ "#BABABA"
  )) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = bonus_score, y = loss_ratio, fill = fill_col)) +
  stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.5, justification = -0.15,
               .width = 0, point_colour = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, outlier.shape = NA,
               show.legend = FALSE, fill = "white",
               colour = "#444444", linewidth = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point",
               shape = 18, size = 3, colour = "black") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "#D6604D",
             linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 1.05,
           label = "Break-even (LR = 1)", hjust = 0,
           colour = "#D6604D", size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_identity() +

       subtitle = "Claimants only (LR > 0), capped at 1.5 | Highlighted: Bad-score policyholders | Diamond = mean",
       x = "Bonus Score", y = "Loss Ratio",
       caption = "< 3% of claimants exceed LR = 1.5 and are excluded") +
  theme_minimal()









Observation: Policyholders with a “Bad” bonus score exhibit substantially higher median loss ratios and greater distributional spread compared to “Good” policyholders, confirming that the bonus-malus system successfully identifies high-risk customers. The “Bad” group contributes disproportionately to portfolio volatility despite representing less than 1% of policies.



6.3 Claim Frequency by Driver Age Group


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(claim_frequency), total_exposure > 0) |>
  mutate(age_group = cut(driver_age,
                          breaks = c(18, 25, 35, 45, 55, 65, 100),
                          labels = c("19-25", "26-35", "36-45",
                                     "46-55", "56-65", "66+"),
                          right = TRUE)) |>
  filter(!is.na(age_group)) |>
  group_by(age_group) |>
  summarise(mean_freq = mean(claim_frequency), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(dot_col = ifelse(age_group == "19-25", "#2166AC", "#BABABA")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = mean_freq)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = age_group, yend = 0.22),
               colour = "#BABABA", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = dot_col), size = 6, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_freq, 3)),
            vjust = -1.0, size = 3.8, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_colour_identity() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0.22, 0.85)) +
  labs(title = "Mean Claim Frequency by Driver Age Group",
       subtitle = "Highlighted: 19-25 group (0.716) files 2.5x more claims than safest 56-65 group (0.289)",
       x = "Driver Age Group", y = "Mean Claim Frequency (claims/policy year)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())









Observation: Claim frequency is highest for the youngest driver age group (19–25), consistent with actuarial research on inexperienced drivers. Frequency gradually decreases for middle-aged drivers (35–55) and slightly increases again for older drivers (65+), forming a characteristic U-shape. This pattern justifies age-based premium differentiation.



6.4 Claim Frequency by Driving Experience Group


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(claim_frequency), total_exposure > 0,
         driving_experience >= 0, driving_experience <= 60) |>
  mutate(exp_group = cut(driving_experience,
                          breaks = c(-1, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 60),
                          labels = c("0-5", "6-10", "11-20",
                                     "21-30", "31-40", "41+"))) |>
  filter(!is.na(exp_group)) |>
  group_by(exp_group) |>
  summarise(mean_freq = mean(claim_frequency), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = exp_group, y = mean_freq)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2166AC", width = 0.65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_freq, 3)),
            vjust = -0.4, size = 3.5) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 0.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(title = "Mean Claim Frequency by Driving Experience Group",
       x = "Years of Driving Experience", y = "Mean Claim Frequency (claims/policy year)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())









Observation: Claim frequency decreases consistently as driving experience increases, with the least experienced drivers (0–5 years) showing the highest frequency. This pattern reinforces the driver age findings and confirms that experience, independent of age, is a meaningful risk predictor. The most experienced drivers (41+ years) show the lowest claim frequency, though this group also tends to be older.



6.5 Loss Ratio by Vehicle Age Group


Show the code

         loss_ratio > 0, loss_ratio <= 1.5) |>

               .width = 0, point_colour = NA, show.legend = FALSE) +

               show.legend = FALSE, fill = "white",
               colour = "#444444", linewidth = 0.6) +

       caption = "< 3% of claimants exceed LR = 1.5 and are excluded") +

Observation: Newer vehicles (0–5 years) show wider loss ratio distributions, possibly driven by higher repair costs or declared values. Very old vehicles (31+ years) show lower and more concentrated loss ratios, likely because they carry lower insured values resulting in smaller absolute claim amounts.



6.6 Claim Severity by Policy Type

Observation: Comprehensive policies (COMP/E: +Excess and COMP/N: Full) show substantially higher claim severity compared to basic coverage types, reflecting their broader protection against costly events like theft and total loss. 7 EDA 5: Bivariate Analysis — Factors Affecting Volatility

7.1 Claim Frequency by Circulation Area and Municipality Type


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(claim_frequency), total_exposure > 0) |>
  group_by(municipality_type, circulation_area) |>
  summarise(mean_freq = mean(claim_frequency), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = municipality_type, y = circulation_area, fill = mean_freq)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_freq, 3)),
            size = 5, fontface = "bold", colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#BABABA", high = "#2166AC",
                      name = "Mean Claim\nFrequency") +
  labs(title = "Mean Claim Frequency by Municipality & Circulation Area — Heatmap",
       subtitle = "Darker blue = higher claim frequency | Inland Urban (0.371) is highest risk combination",
       x = "Municipality Type", y = "Circulation Area") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())









Observation: Urban circulation consistently shows higher claim frequencies than rural across all municipality types, consistent with greater traffic density and accident risk in urban environments. Island municipalities exhibit the highest urban claim frequencies. This geographic segmentation demonstrates that both location type and circulation environment are meaningful predictors of claim volatility.



7.2 Claim Frequency by Vehicle Brand (Top 12)


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(claim_frequency), total_exposure > 0) |>
  group_by(vehicle_brand) |>
  summarise(
    mean_freq = mean(claim_frequency),
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(n >= 500) |>
  slice_max(mean_freq, n = 12) |>
  mutate(vehicle_brand = fct_reorder(vehicle_brand, mean_freq)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = vehicle_brand, y = mean_freq, fill = mean_freq)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(mean_freq, 3)),
            hjust = -0.1, size = 3.2) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.18))) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#90CAF9", high = "#1565C0") +
  labs(title = "Mean Claim Frequency by Vehicle Brand (Top 12)",
       subtitle = "Brands with at least 500 policies only",
       x = NULL, y = "Mean Claim Frequency (claims/policy year)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())









Observation: Claim frequency varies meaningfully across vehicle brands, indicating that brand is a relevant risk factor beyond what is captured by vehicle age and value alone. This variation may reflect differences in driver demographics, vehicle use patterns, or inherent vehicle safety characteristics across brands.



7.3 Loss Ratio Over Time (Year)


Show the code
trend_data <- insurance |>
  filter(!is.na(loss_ratio), total_premium > 0) |>
  group_by(year, policy_type) |>
  summarise(mean_lr = mean(loss_ratio), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(trend_data,
       aes(x = year, y = mean_lr,
           colour = policy_type, group = policy_type,
           linewidth = ifelse(policy_type %in% c("COMP/E: +Excess","COMP/N: Full"), 1.3, 0.7))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "#D6604D", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text_repel(
    data = filter(trend_data, year == 2024),
    aes(label = paste0(policy_type, ": ", round(mean_lr, 2))),
    direction   = "y",
    nudge_x     = 0.12,
    size        = 3,
    show.legend = FALSE,
    segment.color = "grey70",
    segment.size  = 0.3
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(2022, 2023, 2024),
                     expand = expansion(add = c(0.2, 0.9))) +
  scale_linewidth_identity() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "TP: Basic" = "#BABABA", "TPG: +Glass" = "#BABABA",
    "CC: +Add-ons" = "#BABABA", "COMP/E: +Excess" = "#2166AC",
    "COMP/N: Full" = "#2166AC")) +
  labs(title = "Mean Loss Ratio by Policy Type Over Time (2022-2024)",
       subtitle = "COMP/E and COMP/N crossed break-even in 2024",
       x = "Year", y = "Mean Loss Ratio", colour = "Policy Type") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")









Observation: Loss ratios vary across years and policy types. Comprehensive policies consistently sit above basic coverage types throughout the three-year period. Any upward trend could indicate inflationary pressure on claims costs such as rising repair or medical expenses.



7.4 Relationship Between Premium and Incurred Cost


Show the code
insurance |>
  filter(total_incurred > 0, total_premium > 0) |>
  filter(total_premium  <= quantile(total_premium, 0.99),
         total_incurred <= quantile(total_incurred, 0.99)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = total_premium, y = total_incurred,
             colour = policy_type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#B71C1C",
              linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = comma) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "TP: Basic" = "#BABABA", "TPG: +Glass" = "#BABABA",
    "CC: +Add-ons" = "#BABABA", "COMP/E: +Excess" = "#2166AC",
    "COMP/N: Full" = "#2166AC")) +
  labs(title = "Premium vs Incurred Cost (Policies with Claims)",
       subtitle = "Red dashed line = break-even (premium = incurred cost)",
       x = "Total Premium (EUR)", y = "Total Incurred (EUR)",
       colour = "Policy Type") +
  theme_minimal() +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1, size = 2)))









Observation: Most policies with claims fall below the break-even line (incurred < premium), indicating individual profitability. However, a notable cluster of policies exceed the break-even line, representing loss-making contracts. These tend to be clustered among comprehensive policies, confirming that wider coverage generates both higher revenue and higher claims exposure.

8 Summary and Conclusion
This analysis explored the motor vehicle insurance portfolio across 354,140 policies spanning 2022–2024 using univariate and bivariate EDA methods. All 47 variables were examined across 5 EDA sections.
Key findings on profitability:

The portfolio is dominated by CC: +Add-ons and COMP/E: +Excess policy types which carry the highest claim severity
Bonus score (claims history) is a strong predictor of loss ratio. “Bad” policyholders show markedly higher and more variable loss ratios
Comprehensive policies (COMP/E: +Excess, COMP/N: Full) consistently exhibit higher loss ratios than basic coverage types, and both crossed break-even in 2024
Over 88% of policies generate zero claims, creating a highly skewed loss distribution that drives average loss ratios

Key findings on volatility:

Young drivers (19–25) and drivers with less than 5 years of experience show the highest claim frequencies
Urban circulation and island municipalities show the highest claim frequencies across all regions
Vehicle age, municipality type and circulation area all contribute to claim frequency variation
Vehicle brand shows meaningful variation in claim frequency, indicating that brand is a risk factor beyond age and value alone
The heavy right tail in both claim frequency and severity distributions is the primary source of portfolio volatility

panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits=2, prefix="", cex.cor, ...) {

Computing Derived Fields

df <- covid19 %>%
  mutate(rate = Death / Positive) %>%
  mutate(rate.se = sqrt((rate*(1-rate)) / (Positive))) %>%
  filter(rate > 0)

fit.mean <- weighted.mean(df$rate, 1/df$rate.se^2)



Computing Confidence Interval Limits

number.seq <- seq(1, max(df$Positive), 1)
number.ll95 <- fit.mean - 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul95 <- fit.mean + 1.96 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ll999 <- fit.mean - 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
number.ul999 <- fit.mean + 3.29 * sqrt((fit.mean*(1-fit.mean)) / (number.seq)) 
dfCI <- data.frame(number.ll95, number.ul95, number.ll999, 
                   number.ul999, number.seq, fit.mean)

Good morning everyone. Today I will be walking you through an exploratory visual analysis of a real motor insurance portfolio from Spain. The dataset covers three years of policy transactions and gives us a great opportunity to look at what actually drives profitability and claims volatility. We will move through four parts: dataset overview, portfolio composition, profitability analysis, and volatility analysis.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
About the Dataset


Source: Spanish motor insurer microdata
Period: January 2022 – December 2024
Records: 354,140 policy transactions
Variables: 47 across 4 groups



Group
Variables




Policy & Insured
8


Driver & Vehicle
10


Premiums
8


Claims & Incurred
21




Three derived metrics guide analysis:
\[\text{Loss Ratio} = \frac{\text{Incurred}}{\text{Premium}}\]
\[\text{Claim Freq} = \frac{\text{Claims}}{\text{Exposure}}\]
\[\text{Severity} = \frac{\text{Incurred}}{\text{Claims}}\]






Note


Loss Ratio < 1 = Profitable
Loss Ratio > 1 = Unprofitable





This is real anonymised data from a Spanish motor insurer. Each row is one policy in one year. Loss ratio is our profitability measure — below 1 means profitable. Claim frequency tells us how often accidents happen per year of exposure. Severity tells us the average cost per claim when one does occur.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Policy Type Reference Guide








Code
Full Name
Coverage




TP
Third-Party Only
Liability to others only


TPG
Third-Party + Glass
Liability + windscreen


CC
Third-Party + Add-ons
Liability + theft, fire, glass, legal


COMP/E
Comprehensive with Excess
Full coverage, policyholder pays excess


COMP/N
Full Comprehensive
Full coverage, no excess









Note


CC, COMP/E and COMP/N are the three broadest coverage types and together account for 88.2% of the portfolio. These are the focus of our profitability analysis.




Before we look at charts with policy type codes, here is a quick reference guide. TP and TPG are basic policies covering only third-party liability. CC adds several extras like theft, fire and glass on top of liability. COMP with excess means full comprehensive coverage but the policyholder pays the first portion of any claim. Full comprehensive has no such excess. The three broadest types together account for 88.2 percent of all policies.

Only two of 47 variables have any missing values at all. Fuel type is missing for 0.37 percent and vehicle value for 0.14 percent. Both are handled by exclusion. Everything else is complete, which is exceptional for a real-world dataset of this size.

text:
Insight 1: CC Policies Dominate at 57.8%


CC: +Add-ons (third-party + theft, fire, glass) dominates at 57.8% of all policies
COMP/E: +Excess (comprehensive with excess) is second at 25.8%
TP: Basic (third-party only) is rare at just 1.6% — most customers prefer broader coverage


CC policies dominate at 57.8 percent. These combine third-party liability with add-ons like theft and glass cover. COMP/E at 25.8 percent is full comprehensive with an excess. What stands out is how rare basic TP policies are at just 1.6 percent. This tells us the insurer is largely serving customers who want broader protection.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 2: 89.2% Active Policies, 96.4% Good Bonus Score
text:
Insight 2: 89.2% Active Policies, 96.4% Good Bonus Score


89.2% active; cancellation rate of 10.8% warrants monitoring
96.4% of customers have a Good bonus score — excellent claims history
Bad-score customers are only 1.3% but represent elevated risk


89 percent of policies are active and 11 percent cancelled. The bonus score on the right is very positive. 96 percent of customers have a Good score meaning no recent claims. This is great for profitability. The Bad group at 1.3 percent is small but important as a risk segment.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Insight 3: Middle-Aged Drivers, Older Vehicles


Driver age peaks at 40-60 years (mean: 49, median: 48) — experienced, low-risk segment
Vehicle age median is 25 years — an older fleet than typical
Vehicle value median is €24,730; 75th percentile at €32,252


Using density curves with annotated peaks makes the distributions much clearer than histograms. The driver age peaks sharply at 40 to 60 years. Very few young drivers under 25 appear. The vehicle age median is 25 years which is quite old. Vehicle values are mostly in the 15 to 35 thousand euro range, with a long tail of high-value vehicles that can generate very large claims.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Insight 4: Inland-Dominant, Balanced Urban-Rural


64.6% inland, 28.6% coastal, 6.8% islands — reflects Spain’s geography
Urban vs rural split is nearly equal at 53.8% vs 46.2%
64.2% diesel vehicles — relevant for repair cost patterns


The geographic breakdown shows inland dominance at 64.6 percent. Urban and rural circulation are fairly balanced at 54 and 46 percent. Diesel vehicles make up 64 percent of the fleet. These splits matter because urban and rural drivers have very different claim frequencies as we will see in Part 4.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 5: 88.1% of Policies Have Zero Claims
text:
Insight 5: 88.1% of Policies Have Zero Claims


88.1% of policies never file a claim; only 11.9% generate any loss
Among claimants, distribution peaks at LR = 0.1-0.3 and decays toward break-even
9.0% of ALL policies exceed break-even (LR > 1) — these drive total portfolio losses


Two panels tell the full story. On the left, 88.1 percent of policies never filed a single claim. On the right, we see only claimants. The distribution peaks near 0.1 to 0.3 and decays toward break-even. Just 9 percent of all policies exceed LR equals 1. These are the policies that really matter for the portfolio bottom line.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 6: Comprehensive Policies Have Higher Loss Ratios
text:
Insight 6: Comprehensive Policies Have Higher Loss Ratios


COMP/N: Full mean LR = 0.950, median = 0.897 — highest among all policy types
COMP/E: +Excess mean LR = 0.942, median = 0.915 — second highest
TP: Basic mean LR = 0.864, median = 0.676 — narrowest distribution, lowest loss ratio


This raincloud plot from Chapter 9 combines a half-density curve, boxplot, and mean diamond marker in one chart. The blue half-densities for COMP/E and COMP/N are visibly wider and taller than the grey ones. The mean diamond sits above the median box line for all types, showing the right-skew of insurance losses. Comprehensive policies have both higher medians and wider spreads.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 7: Bad Claims History Predicts Higher Loss Ratios
text:
Insight 7: Bad Claims History Predicts Higher Loss Ratios


Bad-score median LR = 0.668, IQR = 0.31–1.05 — wide spread crossing break-even
Good-score median LR = 0.724, IQR = 0.35–1.10 — both groups show high variance
Bad policyholders are only 1.3% of portfolio (n=433) — the half-density shape shows heavier tail risk


The raincloud plot highlights the Bad group in blue. The median difference between Bad and Good is actually modest. What the raincloud reveals is the distribution shape — the half-density for Bad policyholders is wider with a heavier upper tail, meaning more of them have high loss ratios. Both groups have similarly wide IQRs crossing break-even. The bonus-malus system identifies customers who are more likely to generate large claims, even if the average difference is not dramatic.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 8: Comprehensive Policies Cost More Per Claim
text:
Insight 8: Comprehensive Policies Cost More Per Claim


COMP/E: +Excess mean severity = €753 per claim; median = €547 — highest among all types
CC: +Add-ons mean = €651, median = €437 — moderate severity
Wide gap between mean and median across ALL types confirms heavily right-skewed distributions


Comprehensive policies generate not only more claims but also more expensive ones. COMP_E and COMP_N show wider half-density curves at higher severity levels. The large gap between the mean diamond and the median box line across all policy types confirms that a small number of very large claims drive average severity up. This unpredictability is the core source of underwriting risk.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 9: Young Drivers File Claims 2.7x More Often
text:
Insight 9: Young Drivers File Claims 2.7x More Often


19-25 group: mean frequency = 0.716 — highest of all age groups
56-65 group: mean frequency = 0.289 — safest segment
Young drivers file claims 2.5x more often than the 56-65 group (0.716 / 0.289 = 2.48x)


A lollipop chart is cleaner than a bar chart for showing this comparison — less ink, same information, the dot draws the eye straight to the value. The 19-25 group highlighted in blue stands out clearly at 0.716. Then frequency drops steadily through middle age. Young drivers file claims 2.5 times more often than the safest group. Note the 19-25 sample is relatively small as very few young drivers appear in this portfolio.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 10: Urban Areas Drive Higher Claim Frequency
text:
Insight 10: Urban Areas Drive Higher Claim Frequency


Inland Urban = 0.371 — highest claim frequency of all 6 combinations
Urban always exceeds rural within each municipality type — traffic density effect
Island Rural = 0.246 — lowest frequency, well-insulated from traffic risk


A heatmap from Chapter 14 is ideal here — it shows all 6 municipality-circulation combinations in one clean grid. Darker blue means higher claim frequency. Inland Urban at 0.371 is the darkest cell and the highest risk combination. Island Rural at 0.246 is the lightest. The pattern is clear: urban always exceeds rural in every row, and inland urban poses the greatest volatility risk.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
section: Insight 11: COMP/N and COMP/E Crossed Break-Even in 2024
text:
Insight 11: COMP/N and COMP/E Crossed Break-Even in 2024


COMP/N: Full: LR rose from 0.706 (2022) → 0.944 (2023) → 1.171 (2024) — crossed break-even
COMP/E: +Excess: LR rose from 0.641 (2022) → 0.783 (2023) → 1.106 (2024) — also crossed
CC, TP, TPG remain below break-even throughout — basic coverage types stay profitable


This is the most alarming finding in the analysis. COMP/N went from 0.706 in 2022 all the way to 1.171 in 2024. COMP/E similarly crossed from 0.641 to 1.106. Both comprehensive policy types are now paying out more in claims than they collect in premiums. This could be claims inflation from rising repair or medical costs. Basic coverage types CC, TP and TPG remain comfortably below break-even throughout.

title: Motor Vehicle Insurance Portfolio
text:
Key Findings Summary


Profitability

🔵 COMP/N LR: 0.71 → 1.17 (2022-2024)
🔵 COMP/E LR: 0.64 → 1.11 (2022-2024)
⬜ Bad-score policyholders: IQR 0.31-1.05
⬜ 88.1% of policies have zero claims


Volatility

🔵 19-25 drivers: 0.716 claims/yr (2.5x vs safest group)
🔵 Inland Urban: 0.371 claims/yr (highest region)
⬜ Urban always > Rural across all municipality types
⬜ Wide severity IQR across all policy types








Important


Core finding: 88.1% of policies have zero claims. The portfolio’s challenge is that COMP/N and COMP/E (full comprehensive policies) have now crossed break-even — the insurer is losing money on these segments.




To summarise. The biggest story is the trend: COMP/N rose from 0.71 to 1.17 and COMP/E from 0.64 to 1.11 over three years. Both are now loss-making. On the volatility side, young drivers at 0.716 and inland urban areas at 0.371 are the highest-frequency segments. Young drivers file claims 2.5 times more than the 56-65 group. The overarching finding is that 88 percent of policies are fine. The challenge is managing the small but growing share of loss-making comprehensive policies.

title: MC2 Data description
text:
This folder contains the data for the anomalous postings originating from Tenant Thread.
This data is based on the actions taken by the employees and personal agents inside of Tenant Thread.


The anomalous posting is sent to SaidIt by John Windward on May 17, 2046 at 4:21am.



MC2_Data.json – A timeline of events gathered by the internal systems. org_chart.json – The organization chart of Tenant Thread including people and departments. Compatible with networkX node_link_graph.



Derived from data:
{
   "description": "string",
   "events": [
      {
         "short_name": "string",
         "parties": "array",
         "when": "float",
         "details": "object",
         "id": "int"
      }
   ]
}



The data is structured as a timeline. The events are ordered and indicate the operations performed by people, autonomous agents and office systems.
Field meanings: - short_name: The action taken - parties: Which people/agents/systems were involved. - when: Unix timestamp. The challenge occurs in May 2046, and timestamps should be in that month. - details: Additional information about the action taken. The contents vary by the contents of short_name. - id: A unique id for each record.
